actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: Arvicola amphibius has a large range extending from France and the United Kingdom in the west, through much of continental Europe and Russia, as far as the Lena Basin and Lake Baikal in Siberia, Russia. It may be absent from most of mainland Italy where recent genetic work has confirmed the presence of a separate species, A. italicus (Castiglia et al. 2016). Its range extends north of the Arctic circle and south into Iran and the Near East (Shenbrot and Krasnov 2005).
documentation.population: Fossorial monotypes of this species can exhibit large fluctuations over cycles lasting six years or more (Saucy 1999) which are linked to the gradual ageing of populations (Cerqueira et al. 2006). At high population densities, large scale damage to rice fields has been reported in Macedonia (B. Kryštufek pers. comm. 2007). This species is thus considered a pest in some regions. However, in other areas, it has undergone clear declines. For example, it was common in the Hula swamps of Israel until the area was drained in 1957 (Qumsiyeh 1996). In the UK, surveys indicate that the 98.7% of the national population was lost between 1939 and 1998 (Strachan and Jefferies 1993, Stachan et al. 2000) and the remaining population further declined by 50% between 1999 and 2017 (Mathews et al. 2018). Local-level declines have also previously been reported in the Netherlands (Norren et al. 2020).
documentation.habitats: This large vole can exhibit considerable ecological adaptation and has been reported to occur as aquatic and fossorial morphotypes (Wilson et al. 2017) that were previously regarded as separate species (Chevret et al. 2020). It survives in a range of habitats around rivers, streams and marshes in the lowlands and the mountains (Harrison and Bates 1991), though can also occupy dry grasslands (Wijas et al. 2023) and urban habitats (Leivesley et al. 2021). Its presence can be influenced by habitat, proximity to colonies that act as source populations, and occupancy of American Mink (Neovison vison) which is known to predate on this species (Brzeziński et al. 2019). It is active during the day and night, but primarily at dawn and dusk (Wilson et al. 2017). It feeds mostly on vegetation, but also consumes some insects, crustaceans, molluscs, and small fish, and roots, bulbs and tubers in the winter (Reichstein 1982, Harrison and Bates 1991). Reproduction occurs during the warmer months of the year and may begin as early as March, with gestation lasting 20-30 days and 4-6 young produced per litter (Wilson et al. 2017).
documentation.threats: Declines in aquatic populations in parts of western Europe have been attributed to predation by introduced American Mink, habitat loss and fragmentation, and water pollution (Rushton et al. 2000). Population fragmentation is more pronounced in Mediterranean populations due to increased aridity. Local population extinctions and reductions have occurred in Turkey, Georgia and other parts of this range due to drainage of swamp habitat (Qumsiyeh 1996). It is considered an agricultural pest and extensive control measures are carried out in some areas.
documentation.measures: The species occurs in protected areas throughout its range. Recovery projects have been undertaken in the UK focusing on habitat enhancements, sympathetic site management, reintroductions and American Mink monitoring and control (e.g. Moorhouse et al. 2015). Further research of its complex taxonomy, population trends and threats is needed.
documentation.rationale: The Eurasian Water Vole has a wide distribution range with a very large extent of occurrence (EOO). The population size has not been quantified, but it is not believed to approach the thresholds for the population size criterion of the IUCN Red List (i.e. fewer than 10,000 mature individuals in conjunction with appropriate decline rates and subpopulation qualifiers). Although it has experienced significant reductions in some parts of its range (such as in the United Kingdom), population trends elsewhere are believed to be stable. It is therefore assessed as Least Concern, but conservation and monitoring efforts are required in regions where it is declining.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Linnaeus' amphibius and terrestris, both proposed in 1758 on the same page, are now considered conspecific by most researchers. As shown by Corbet (1978), amphibius has a priority over terrestris, based on Blasius (1857) as the first reviser. 

At one point, this species was split into A. amphibius and A. scherman (Panteleyev 2001). Arvicola amphibius is larger, with shaggy pelage and ortodont incisors, and is associated with aquatic environments; A. scherman is smaller, with softer pelage, more reduced plantar and palmar tubercles, and the upper incisors strongly projecting forwards and has fossorial habits (Panteleyev 2001).

However, the taxonomy of the A. amphibius group is more complex. Considering genetic distances and other biological data, it is suggested that the Italian lineage corresponds to a separate species (Arvicola italicus; Castiglia et al. 2016). The three other lineages correspond to phylogeographic variations of a single species (A. amphibius), encompassing the former A. amphibius, Arvicola terrestris, Arvicola scherman, and Arvicola monticola (Chevret et al. 2020, Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022).
